name: STM32H503RBT6
title: Arm Cortex-M33 250 MHz microcontroller, 128 KB flash, 32 KB SRAM, I3C, USB, FDCAN, 1.71 V to 3.6 V
summary: A 250 MHz Arm Cortex-M33 microcontroller with FPU, an 8 KB instruction cache, 128 Kbytes of dual-bank ECC flash, 32 Kbytes of SRAM and 2 Kbytes of battery-backed SRAM, running from 1.71 V to 3.6 V. It brings a 2.5 Msps 12-bit ADC, a two-channel 12-bit DAC, a comparator and an op amp, two I2C and two I3C, three USARTs and an LPUART, three SPI/I2S, FDCAN, full-speed USB host and device, a hash accelerator and true RNG, and an RTC with tamper detection. Packages run from WLCSP25 to LQFP64. STM32H503RBT6 is the LQFP64 part with 49 I/Os for -40 °C to 85 °C ambient.
key_figures: Arm Cortex-M33 with FPU, up to 250 MHz, 375 DMIPS, 1023 CoreMark
128 Kbytes flash (2 banks, ECC), 32 Kbytes SRAM, 2 Kbytes backup SRAM, 2 Kbytes OTP
VDD 1.71 V to 3.6 V; VDDIO2 down to 1.08 V (WLCSP25); VBAT 1.2 V to 3.6 V
25.5 mA typ at 250 MHz from flash, VOS0, all peripherals off
54 µA typ (SVOS5) / 2.91 µA typ at 3 V / 0.02 µA typ at 3 V
HSI 64 MHz, HSI48, CSI 4 MHz, LSI 32 kHz

circuits.title: Power supply scheme (LQFP64, LDO on)
circuits.description: The LQFP64 supplies with the internal regulator running. VDD feeds the four VDD pins, each with its own 100 nF, and a 4.7 µF bulk capacitor on the rail. The two VCAP pins carry the core regulator output and take 2.2 µF each. VDDA/VREF+ gets 1 µF and 100 nF to VSSA/VREF-. VBAT runs from a backup battery with 1 µF and 100 nF.
notes: VBAT may instead be tied to VDD, keeping its 100 nF.
With the LDO off (bypass), the VCAP pins are fed from an external VCORE supply, tied together, with 100 nF at each in place of 2.2 µF.
On WLCSP25 the VDDIO2 ball takes 100 nF, plus 1 µF, and may be its own supply or tied to VDD; packages with one VCAP pin use 4.7 µF there.

circuits.title: 8 MHz crystal on the HSE oscillator
circuits.description: An 8 MHz crystal sits between OSC_IN and OSC_OUT with a load capacitor from each side to ground; the feedback resistor RF is inside the chip. REXT in series with OSC_OUT is chosen to suit the crystal. CL1 and CL2 are normally equal ceramics of 5 pF to 20 pF, picked so that their series value plus about 10 pF of stray capacitance meets the crystal's load.
notes: A resonator with built-in capacitors replaces Y1, C1 and C2.

circuits.title: 32.768 kHz crystal on the LSE oscillator
circuits.description: A 32.768 kHz crystal between OSC32_IN and OSC32_OUT, with a load capacitor from each side to ground, placed close to the pins. The feedback resistor is inside, and no resistor may be added across the crystal.
notes: A resonator with built-in capacitors replaces Y1, C1 and C2.

circuits.title: NRST pin protection
circuits.description: A push-button pulls NRST to ground for a manual reset, and 0.1 µF from NRST to ground keeps noise from causing stray resets. The pull-up RPU is inside the chip.
notes: The level on NRST must be able to fall below VIL(NRST) maximum, or the reset is not taken.

circuits.title: ADC input connection on an FT/TT pin
circuits.description: A signal source with output resistance RAIN drives an ADC-capable pin; Cparasitic is the board plus pad capacitance at the pin. RAIN must stay within the limit for the chosen resolution and sampling time, and a large Cparasitic calls for a lower ADC clock.
notes: PA0 (ADC1_INP0) is shown; every ADC input connects the same way.

circuits.title: Analog supply and reference decoupling
circuits.description: VREF+ is bonded to VDDA and VREF- to VSSA inside, so one pair of pins carries both. A 1 µF and a 100 nF in parallel go from VDDA/VREF+ to VSSA/VREF-, as close to the chip as possible; the 100 nF is a good-quality ceramic.

operation.text: An Arm Cortex-M33 with single-precision FPU and DSP instructions, running up to 250 MHz. It has an eight-region MPU and two AHB ports: C-AHB for the code region and S-AHB for SRAM, peripherals and the Vendor_SYS region. Benchmarks: 1.5 DMIPS/MHz (Dhrystone 2.1), 375 DMIPS, 1023 CoreMark (4.092 CoreMark/MHz).

An 8-Kbyte instruction cache sits on the C-AHB bus and lets code run from flash with no wait state at up to 250 MHz. A hit costs no wait state; a miss refills the line by AHB burst with the critical word first, and new requests are served during a refill. It is two-way set-associative with pLRU-t replacement, can be set direct-mapped to save power, counts hits and misses, can cache four remapped external regions, and flags an unexpected cacheable write with an optional interrupt.

The MPU divides memory into up to eight protected regions so one task cannot overwrite memory or resources of another; an access to a forbidden location is caught and can be handled by an RTOS, which may reprogram the regions per task.

128 Kbytes in two banks, each of eight 8-Kbyte pages; one bank can be read while the other is erased or programmed. A 2-Kbyte one-time-programmable area holds user data. ECC covers all non-volatile memory: single errors are corrected, double errors detected and the failing address reported. Option bytes set the product state (debug access protection), up to two write-protected areas per bank at 8-Kbyte granularity, sector-group write protection covering as many as 32 groups per bank, each four sectors or 32 Kbytes, and one hide-protection (HDP) area per bank that isolates start-up code. Each sector can be set privileged or unprivileged at run time.

SRAM1 (16 Kbytes) and SRAM2 (16 Kbytes) are the main RAMs; BKPSRAM is 2 Kbytes kept in every low-power mode and in VBAT mode with VDD off. All three have ECC, which is off by default and is turned on by clearing the option bits SRAM1_ECC, SRAM2_ECC and BKPRAM_ECC. Blocks of SRAM1 and SRAM2 can be powered down in Stop mode. SRAM1 and SRAM2 privilege is set per 512-byte page through the MPCBB; backup SRAM privilege is set by a watermark in the GTZC.

BOOT0 chooses at start-up between user flash and the system bootloader. From user flash the start address is NSBOOTADD, which NSBOOT_LOCK can freeze. The bootloader, stored in system memory at the factory, reprograms the flash over USART, I2C, I3C, SPI, FDCAN or USB device (DFU). Debug authentication, started from ST tools with a password, can launch a full regression of the product.

Two sub-blocks with separate 32-bit AHB interfaces: TZSC sets the privilege state of peripherals and bus masters and the size of the watermark-protected backup SRAM area, and tells RCC and the GPIOs which peripherals are privileged; MPCBB sets the privilege of each 512-byte page of internal SRAM.

VDD, 1.71 V to 3.6 V, feeds the I/Os, the regulator and the system analog (reset, power management, internal clocks). VDDA feeds the ADC, DAC, op amp and comparator and is independent of VDD: its floor is 1.62 V for the ADC and comparator, 1.8 V for the DAC and 2.0 V for the op amp, up to 3.6 V; with those blocks unused it is best tied to VDD. VDDIO2, 1.08 V to 3.6 V, supplies nine I/Os (PA8, PA9, PA15, PB3 to PB8) and exists as a separate pin only on WLCSP25; unused, it is best tied to VDD. VBAT, 1.2 V to 3.6 V, keeps the RTC, the 32 kHz oscillator and the backup registers alive through a switch when VDD is absent. VREF+ and VREF- have no pins: inside they are bonded to VDDA and VSSA.

An internal LDO makes VCORE for the logic, SRAM1, SRAM2 and flash, on the VCAP pin, which takes external capacitance of 2 x 2.2 µF typical. It offers four voltage scales and keeps running in Stop mode. Run mode scales: VOS0 and VOS1 for highest performance, VOS2 balanced, VOS3 lowest consumption. Stop mode scales: SVOS3 keeps wakeup-capable peripherals (UART, SPI, I2C, LPTIM) running; SVOS4 and SVOS5 keep a reduced set that still includes GPIO wakeup through EXTI.

VCORE can be supplied from outside with the LDO turned off. The LDO is on after power-up, so the external VCORE must first settle above 1.1 V and stay there until software turns the LDO off; after that the external voltage may be set to what the application needs.

While VDD is under 1 V, VDDA and VDDIO2 must stay below VDD + 300 mV. Above 1 V on VDD the supplies are independent. During power-down VDD may briefly fall below the other supplies provided the energy delivered to the chip stays under 1 mJ, so decoupling capacitors may discharge at different rates.

POR and PDR hold the device in reset while VDD is under a fixed threshold. The BOR, turned on by the BORH_EN option bit, offers three thresholds between 2.1 V and 2.7 V set in option bytes. The PVD compares VDD with a selectable threshold, or the PVD_IN pin with VREFINT, and interrupts on falling and/or rising crossings; software enables it. The AVD does the same for VDDA. IO2VM watches VDDIO2. VBAT is compared with two thresholds, and a dedicated sensor compares the junction temperature with two thresholds.

After any reset the device is in Run mode. Sleep stops only the CPU; peripherals keep running and any interrupt or event wakes it. Stop keeps SRAM and registers, stops every clock in the VCORE domain and turns off the PLLs, CSI, HSI, HSI48 and HSE; LSE or LSI keeps running and the RTC may stay on. On leaving Stop the system clock is HSI (up to 64 MHz) or CSI (4 MHz), chosen by software. Standby is the lowest-power mode with BOR kept on: PLL, HSI, CSI, HSI48 and HSE off, the RTC optional, I/O states may be held, and everything is lost except the backup domain (registers and backup SRAM) and the standby circuitry. Standby ends on NRST, an IWDG reset, a WKUP pin edge (rising or falling, selectable), an RTC alarm, periodic wakeup or timestamp, or a tamper event from a pin or an internal fault; the clock after wakeup is HSI at 32 MHz.
During and after reset the I/Os are in analog state with their Schmitt triggers off, which lowers consumption under reset. After reset every GPIO is in analog mode.

VBAT may come from a battery or a supercapacitor. It powers the RTC with the LSE, the tamper logic, the backup registers and the 2-Kbyte backup SRAM, with two tamper pins active. The switch to VBAT is automatic when VDD disappears. A built-in charger for the VBAT source can be enabled while VDD is present. In VBAT mode neither external interrupts nor RTC alarms or events bring the device out of it.
Some peripherals are wired to each other directly so they can trigger one another without the CPU, with fixed, short latency; depending on the peripheral this works in Run and Sleep modes.

SYSCLK comes from one of four sources: HSE (4 MHz to 50 MHz crystal or ceramic resonator, or an external clock in bypass), HSI (64 MHz RC, software-trimmed), CSI (4 MHz low-power RC, software-trimmed), or the system PLL fed by any of those three, up to 250 MHz. HSI48 (48 MHz RC with clock recovery) can clock the USB. The RTC runs from LSE (32.768 kHz crystal with four drive levels, or an external clock in bypass) or LSI (32 kHz RC, which also clocks the IWDG). Two PLLs with two outputs each give independent kernel clocks to the ADC, USB, RNG and FDCAN1. After reset the core runs from HSI at 32 MHz. The clock security system moves SYSCLK to HSI when the HSE fails and can interrupt; an LSE failure can also interrupt. MCO puts an internal clock on a pin; LSCO puts out LSI or LSE in every low-power mode except Standby and VBAT. AHB and APB domains run up to 250 MHz.

The CRS trims HSI48 automatically against a reference: the USB start-of-frame, the LSE, a signal on the CRS_SYNC pin, or software. Manual and automatic trimming can be combined to lock faster at start-up.

Each pin is set by software as push-pull or open-drain output, input (floating, pulled up or pulled down), or alternate function; most share digital or analog functions. The alternate-function setting can be locked by a fixed write sequence. The high-speed low-voltage mode (HSLV) raises I/O speed at low supply and is needed for interfaces such as SPI there; it may be used only with VDD or VDDIO2 under 2.7 V and is turned on by the IO_VDD_HSLV or IO_VDDIO2_HSLV option bit together with the HSLVx bits.

A 32-bit multi-AHB matrix connects the CPU, GPDMA1 and GPDMA2 to flash, SRAM and the AHB and APB peripherals. Each GPDMA has two AHB master ports and eight channels, each with its own FIFO, moving data memory-to-memory, memory-to-peripheral, peripheral-to-memory or peripheral-to-peripheral, also in Sleep mode. Transfers follow linked lists in memory (run-to-completion or link-step), with byte reordering, packing, padding, sign extension and realignment; some channels address in 2D for scatter-gather and interleaving. Priority has one high-priority class (queue 3) and three weighted round-robin classes (queues 0 to 2). Each channel raises events and interrupts on transfer complete, half transfer, errors and suspension, and can be privileged or not.

The NVIC has 16 priority levels and up to 134 maskable channels plus the 16 Cortex-M33 lines, with tail chaining and late-arrival handling. The EXTI has up to 54 lines, each able to wake the system from Stop, with selectable edge, separate rising and falling pending bits, per-line interrupt and event masks, software triggers and the I/O port multiplexer.
Computes a CRC with a programmable polynomial and size, for checking transmitted or stored data; under EN/IEC 60335-1 it is one way to verify flash contents against a signature made at link time.

One 12-bit successive-approximation ADC up to 2.5 Msps, single-ended or differential inputs, injected channels, hardware offset calibration, offset and gain compensation, oversampling up to x1024, a 32-bit data register, DMA and three analog watchdogs. Inside it converts the temperature sensor, VREFINT and VBAT through a divide-by-4 bridge, so the result is a quarter of VBAT.

An analog sensor gives a voltage linear in temperature to an ADC channel; its offset differs from chip to chip, so it must be calibrated for absolute readings, and each part carries factory calibration values in read-only system memory. A digital sensor (DTS) turns temperature into a square wave whose frequency rises with temperature, measured against PCLK or LSE; RM0492 gives the conversion. VREFINT is a bandgap output for the ADC and comparator; its exact voltage is measured on each part and stored in system memory.

One 12-bit voltage-output DAC with two channels, each with its own converter; 8-bit or 12-bit, left- or right-aligned in 12-bit mode. The channels convert independently or together with synchronised update. It generates noise, triangle and sawtooth waves, has per-channel DMA with underrun detection and double-data DMA, external triggers, an optional output buffer with offset calibration for higher drive, and a sample-and-hold mode for low power in Stop mode. Each output can be cut from its pin and routed to on-chip peripherals, leaving the pin free as a GPIO.

COMP1 has programmable hysteresis, speed (low speed for low power) and output polarity. Its reference input is an I/O, a DAC channel, VREFINT or 1/4, 1/2 or 3/4 of it, the temperature sensor or VBAT/4. It can wake the device from Stop, interrupt, and drive timer break inputs.

OPAMP1 has two inputs and one output on pins and can run as a follower or as a PGA with internal gain: non-inverting 2, 4, 8 or 16, inverting -1, -3, -7 or -15. Its positive input can come from the DAC and its output goes to the ADC inside. Input bias as low as 1 nA, offset as low as 1.5 mV, and a gain-bandwidth product reaching 7 MHz. OPAMP1_VINM has no ball on WLCSP25.

A true RNG with an analog entropy source and a conditioning stage approved under NIST SP800-90B, giving 32-bit words; usable as the entropy source of a nondeterministic random bit generator. It delivers four 32-bit samples every 412 AHB clocks when fAHB is under 77 MHz, otherwise every 256 RNG clocks. Start-up and continuous health tests (repetition count, adaptive proportion) are built in. It accepts 32-bit word accesses only; others cause an AHB bus error and writes are ignored. It can be turned off or left in its default automatic low-power mode.

Hardware SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256 and HMAC, to FIPS PUB 180-4, FIPS PUB 186-4, RFC 2104 and FIPS PUB 198-1. One 512-bit block takes 82 clocks with SHA-1 and 66 with SHA-256. Padding to 512 bits is automatic; input goes through one 32-bit register into a sixteen-word FIFO, with bit, byte, half-word or word swapping; the digest is eight 32-bit words H0 to H7. One DMA channel (single or burst of 4) feeds it, word accesses only, and a computation can be suspended and resumed with reloadable digest registers.

TIM1 is the advanced-control timer: 16-bit, four channels with complementary outputs and programmable dead time, usable as three-phase PWM over six outputs; in debug its counter can be frozen and its PWM outputs turned off so driven power switches are safe. TIM2 (32-bit counter and prescaler) and TIM3 (16-bit) are general-purpose: four channels each (capture, compare, PWM, one-pulse output), quadrature encoder input, DMA requests, and synchronisation with other timers through the timer link. TIM6 and TIM7 are 16-bit basic timers, mainly for triggering the DAC or as plain time bases.

LPTIM1 and LPTIM2 have their own clock and keep counting in Stop mode when run from LSE, LSI or an external clock, and can wake the system from Stop. Each has a 16-bit up-counter with auto-reload and compare registers, a 3-bit prescaler (1 to 128 in powers of two), clock from LSE, LSI, HSI, the APB clock or an external input (which counts pulses with no oscillator running), continuous or one-shot mode, hardware or software trigger, a digital glitch filter, pulse or PWM output with selectable polarity, encoder mode, a repetition counter, up to two channels for capture, edge-aligned PWM or one-pulse output, interrupts on 10 events, and DMA on update and capture.

The IWDG has a 12-bit down-counter and 8-bit prescaler clocked by the 32 kHz LSI, independent of the main clock, so it runs in Stop and Standby; it resets the device or serves as a free-running timeout, is started by hardware or software as set in the option bytes, and can be frozen in debug. The WWDG has a 7-bit down-counter on the main clock with an early-warning interrupt, also freezable in debug. SysTick is the Cortex-M33's 24-bit auto-reload down-counter with an interrupt at zero and a selectable clock.

BCD calendar with sub-seconds, 12- or 24-hour format, weekday, date, month and year with automatic month-length and leap-year correction, or a 32-bit binary free-running counter. Two alarms, a 17-bit auto-reload wakeup timer, timestamp on a pin event, a tamper event or the switch to VBAT, shift correction of 1 to 32767 RTC clock pulses for synchronising to a master clock, reference clock detection from a 50 Hz or 60 Hz source, and digital calibration with 0.95 ppm resolution. It is powered from VDD or, without VDD, from VBAT. Clock: LSE crystal, LSE resonator or oscillator, LSI (32 kHz typical), or HSE divided in the RCC. With LSE it runs in VBAT mode and every low-power mode; with LSI it runs in every low-power mode but not in VBAT mode. Every RTC event can interrupt and wake the device; alarms, wakeup timer and timestamp each have privilege protection.

32 backup registers of 32 bits sit in the backup domain and are kept in every low-power mode and in VBAT mode. Up to two tamper pins detect edges or levels (with filtering and internal pull-up handling) or run as active tampers that check the line is neither opened nor shorted. Eleven internal tamper sources: backup-domain voltage, temperature, LSE and HSE monitoring, overflow of the RTC calendar, debug (JTAG/SWD) access when the product state is not 0, ADC analog watchdogs, monotonic counter overflow, an RNG fault, an IWDG reset with a tamper flag already set, and system fault detection. On a tamper, the device can wipe backup registers, backup SRAM, SRAM2 and the I-cache, at once in hardware mode or by software in software mode, and any tamper can timestamp the RTC. A monotonic counter is included.

Two I2C interfaces, to I2C-bus specification rev. 5: master, slave and multimaster; Standard-mode to 100 kbit/s, Fast-mode to 400 kbit/s and Fast-mode Plus to 1 Mbit/s with 20 mA drive I/Os; 7-bit and 10-bit addresses, more than one 7-bit own address, adjustable setup and hold timing, clock stretching that can be turned off. SMBus 3.0 (hardware PEC with ACK control, address resolution protocol, alert) and PMBus 1.3. An independent kernel clock keeps the bit rate fixed when PCLK changes; analog and digital noise filters; wakeup from Stop; a one-byte buffer with DMA.

Two I3C interfaces to MIPI I3C v1.1, acting as controller or target, on the same I/Os as I2C1 and I2C2. As controller it can share the bus with legacy I2C targets in Fast-mode or Fast-mode Plus that do not stretch the clock. It works with DMA.

USART1, USART2 and USART3 offer full-duplex asynchronous NRZ communication with a fractional baud-rate generator, oversampling by 16 or 8, auto baud rate, 7, 8 or 9 data bits, MSB- or LSB-first, 1 or 2 stop bits, 8-byte transmit and receive FIFOs, synchronous master or slave mode (so each can act as an SPI), single-wire half-duplex, LIN (13-bit break send, 10 or 11-bit break detect), IrDA SIR (3/16 bit in normal mode), smartcard T=0 and T=1 to ISO/IEC 7816-3 with 0.5 and 1.5 stop bits, Modbus timeout and CR/LF detection, CTS/RTS and RS-485 driver enable, swappable TX and RX, polarity control, DMA, and wakeup from Stop. Up to 20 Mbaud with DMA. LPUART1 keeps asynchronous, half-duplex, flow control, FIFOs, DMA and Stop wakeup but drops synchronous, smartcard, IrDA, LIN, Modbus, receiver timeout and auto-baud; on the 32.768 kHz LSE alone it runs 300 baud to 9600 baud, so it can wait for a frame in Stop mode, and a faster clock gives higher rates.

Three SPIs, each also an I2S. SPI: master or slave, full-duplex on three lines, half-duplex on two with a bidirectional line, simplex, 4-bit to 32-bit frames, multimaster or multislave, an independent kernel clock, baud prescaler up to kernel clock / 2 or bypass in master mode, hardware or software SS with programmable polarity and timing, MISO and MOSI swap, Motorola and TI formats, hardware CRC with a 5-bit to 33-bit polynomial, 16 x 8-bit FIFOs with DMA and threshold packing, an optional RDY status line from the slave, and wakeup from Stop. I2S: master or slave, full-duplex or simplex, 16, 24 or 32-bit data, 16 or 32-bit channel length as master and any as slave, Philips, MSB-justified, LSB-justified and PCM (short or long frame sync), an 8-bit linear prescaler, underrun, overrun and frame error flags, DMA, and a master clock output fixed at 256 x FWS. The audio clock comes from a PLL or an external input.

One CAN controller to ISO 11898-1:2015 (CAN 2.0 A and B) and CAN FD 1.0, with up to 64 data bytes, a shared 0.8-Kbyte message RAM for filters and FIFOs, two receive FIFOs of three payloads, a three-payload transmit FIFO or queue, a transmit event FIFO, high-priority message signalling, error logging, AUTOSAR and J1939 support, loop-back test mode and power-down support. The bus interface (APB) and the CAN core run in separate clock domains.

USB 2.0 full-speed host and device with 2048 bytes of dedicated buffer SRAM (32-bit access), 1 to 8 endpoints, isochronous and double-buffered bulk or isochronous endpoints, suspend and resume, link power management, Battery Charging 1.2 detection as a device, and an internal pull-up on USB_DP switched by software to connect and disconnect.

A combined serial-wire and JTAG debug port: SWD needs two pins (SWDIO shared with JTMS, SWCLK with JTCK); a set sequence on TMS switches between JTAG-DP and SW-DP, and unused JTAG pins become GPIOs. An Arm Embedded Trace Macrocell streams compressed instruction and data trace through a few pins to an external trace port analyser. Debug access can be authenticated.

Voltages are referred to VSS. Minimum and maximum values hold over the worst temperature, supply and frequency, tested on every part at TJ = 25 °C and TJmax; figures marked as characterization or design are not production tested, characterization limits being the mean ±3σ. Typical values are at TJ = 25 °C and VDD = VDDA = 3.3 V. Typical ADC accuracy covers 95 % of parts (mean ±2σ). Pin parameters are measured with 50 pF on the pin.

Every supply and its ground (VDD with VSS, VDDA with VSSA, etc.) need ceramic filter capacitors as close as possible to the pins or under them on the back of the board; leaving them out can make the device misbehave. The values are 100 nF at each VDD pin plus 4.7 µF on VDD, 1 µF and 100 nF on VDDA, 100 nF (and 1 µF) on VDDIO2, 100 nF plus 1 µF with a battery on VBAT, and on VCAP 2.2 µF at each of two pins or 4.7 µF at a single pin. AN5711 has more on board design.

IDD figures are the total current of the chip: VDD, VDDIO2, VDDA and VBAT together, with the LDO on. Run-mode figures use CoreMark code, all I/Os in analog input mode, peripherals off unless stated, the minimum flash wait states for fHCLK, and fPCLK = fHCLK when peripherals run. Peripheral figures are the difference between one peripheral clocked and none, at 250 MHz (VOS0), 200 MHz (VOS1), 150 MHz (VOS2) and 100 MHz (VOS3).

An input with pull-up draws current through the pull-up when held low. An input left at an intermediate level draws current through its Schmitt trigger; analog mode avoids it, and ADC inputs should be in analog mode. Floating inputs can drift or toggle with noise, so unused pins are set to analog mode or held at a fixed level by a pull or by output mode. A toggling output draws ISW = VDDx × fSW × CL.

GPIOs sink or source up to ±8 mA, and up to ±20 mA with relaxed VOL and VOH. The current of all I/Os on VDD plus the chip's Run current must stay within ΣIVDD, and likewise for VSS and ΣIVSS. Every I/O is CMOS and TTL compatible without configuration, except BOOT0.

In HSE bypass the oscillator is off and OSC_IN takes an external clock, digital or low-swing analog; with a low-swing clock the clock squarer must be turned on (RM0492). The LSE bypass works the same way on OSC32_IN.

The HSE runs a 4 MHz to 50 MHz crystal or ceramic resonator between OSC_IN and OSC_OUT with on-chip feedback resistor RF (200 kΩ) and bias-controlled gain. CL1 and CL2 are high-quality ceramic capacitors, usually equal, typically 5 pF to 20 pF, chosen so that their series value plus about 10 pF of pin and board capacitance matches the crystal's rated load. A series resistor REXT at OSC_OUT is sized from the crystal data. Start-up takes about 2 ms; up to 10 mA flows during the first two thirds of it. AN2867 covers crystal choice.

The LSE runs a 32.768 kHz crystal between OSC32_IN and OSC32_OUT with load capacitors to ground, placed as close to the pins as possible to limit distortion and start-up time. No resistor may be added between OSC32_IN and OSC32_OUT. Four drive levels are set by LSEDRV[1:0], from 333 nA (medium-low) to 747 nA (high); start-up takes about 2 s.

NRST has an internal pull-up and a filter. An external network of a push-button to ground and 0.1 µF from NRST to ground guards against stray resets; whatever drives NRST must pull it below its VIL maximum or the reset is ignored.

Below VDDA = 2.7 V the analog switch booster must be used. The source impedance RAIN and the board capacitance limit the sampling time (minimum-sampling-time table); a large parasitic capacitance costs accuracy, which a lower fADC recovers. Negative current injected into one analog input significantly spoils conversions on other inputs, so a Schottky diode from such a pin to ground is advised; positive injection within the IINJ limits has no effect. Slow channels are every ADC input other than the fast ones.
VDDA/VREF+ is decoupled to VSSA/VREF- with 1 µF in parallel with 100 nF good-quality ceramic, as close to the chip as possible.

Measured on LQFP64 at 3.3 V, 25 °C and 250 MHz: ESD on I/Os (IEC 61000-4-2) class 2B and fast transient bursts through 100 pF on VDD and VSS class 5A. A series resistor of about 1 kΩ near the MCU is advised on pins wired to tracks longer than 50 mm. Emission (IEC 61967-2, LQFP64, 3.6 V, 8 MHz HSE, 250 MHz CPU) peaks at 23 dBµV between 130 MHz and 1 GHz, EMI level 3.5. Software should handle runaway conditions (corrupt program counter, unexpected reset, corrupt control registers); forcing NRST or the oscillator pins low for 1 s reproduces the common failures. ESD: 2000 V HBM (class 2), 500 V CDM (class C2a); latch-up class II level A at 130 °C.

Injection into I/Os, by voltages below VSS or above VDD, is to be avoided in normal use. In characterization one floating input at a time is injected while the device runs; a failure is an ADC error over 5 LSB TUE, leakage on neighbouring pins outside -5 µA to +0 µA, or another malfunction such as a reset or oscillator shift. PA4, PA5 and PB1 tolerate no injection; PB10 and PC6 no negative injection; other I/Os 5 mA negative.
The I3C meets MIPI I3C v1.1 timing, SDR only, as controller or target, with SCL up to 12.5 MHz.

The full-speed transceiver needs VDD of 3.0 V to 3.6 V for full electrical compliance; it works down to 2.7 V with degraded figures. The driver includes its matching impedance, so DP and DM need no series resistors.
